title: Tools
text:
WRF’s components
This is a brief outline. Read the user guide for more details.
WRF is made up of two main components: the WRF Preprocessing System (WPS) and the actual WRF model.
WPS includes:

geogrid: sets up the domain projection and ingests static fields from WPS-GEOG; creates geo_em.d01.nc, plus others if using nested domains
ungrib: processes grib files into some kind of intermediary format for WRF by extracting variables listed in the linked Vtable (e.g. Vtable.GFS); produces files like FILE:2019-01-01_00 for each time in the input data
metgrid: combines the geogrid and ungrib outputs into met_em.* NetCDF files

WRF has multiple parts too, only two of which are useful for most people:

real: vertically interpolates the metgrid output (which is still on the same levels as the input data) to the specified model levels and creates wrfinput and wrfbdy files containing ICs and BCs respectively
wrf: this is where you finally run the model - yay!

WRF’s code is a mess, so I wouldn’t recommend diving into understanding it unless you have to. Instead, make sure to read pages like WRF Physics which include information on WRF’s schemes and options.

title: Tools
text:
Installation
The tutorial and user guide provide decent instructions on compiling and running case studies.
You can decide whether you install your own versions of the WRF dependencies (like NetCDF) which the tutorial guides you through or use one installed on your system (e.g. CX3) if available. The benefit of using pre-installed ones is that you don’t have to struggle with inter-library and system compatibility. You don’t have to use MPICH as in the WRF tutorial; Open MPI also works and is the only one which works on CX3.
You must install WPS in order to run WRF with “real” data.

title: Tools
text:
Using ERA5 as input data
GFS is the most common input data with which to run WRF, but ERA5 also works. As of 2026, the ECMWF Vtable is out of date, plus you need a file containing ERA5’s invariant fields (unless you download land mask, soil height, and soil geopotential with your ERA5 data) and an updated METGRID.TBL to do SST and skintemp interpolation correctly. All of these materials can be found here.

title: Tools
text:
Troubleshooting
This is a non-exhaustive list of the most common issues encountered with WRF. Please add as you see fit, but only remove if you are certain the issue is no longer relevant.

Libraries

netcdf.inc doesn’t exist (required for library compatibility tests): NetCDF hasn’t built properly, look in the output.
General installation issues:

Ensure FCFLAGS and FFLAGS are "-m64 -fallow-argument-mismatch".
Ensure LDFLAGS points to library folders "-L$NETCDF/lib -L$DIR/grib2/lib".
Ensure CPPFLAGS points to include folders "-I$NETCDF/include -I$DIR/mpich/include -I$DIR/grib2/include -fcommon".

gcc: error: unrecognized command line option '-V': probably GCC version issue, never got to the bottom of it.
There’s a million and one problems, just keep reading the logs and googling.
Lots of problems are caused by library compatibilities with GCC, 12.3.0 worked in the end.



Compiling WRF and WPS

Fails because number of CPUs exceeded: default is 2 so do ncpus=2 and add -j 2 to the command.
If reconfiguring/recompiling, run ./clean -a before ./configure.
General compilation issues:

Ensure same GCC version is used for libraries and compilation.




Running WPS
Ungrib issues:

Check the correct Vtable is linked by doing realpath Vtable in the WPS folder. Should show the path to the true Vtable.
Use ungrib.log to see which variables have been identified.

Geogrid issues:

Geogrid fails with ERROR: Error in ext_pkg_write_field (if namelist.wps has debug_level=1000, may also see WRF_DEBUG: NetCDF error: Operation not permitted): NetCDF hadn’t installed properly, check the library installation logs better! Even when it says “congratulations library installed”, sometimes things have failed.

Metgrid issues:

Ensure it’s reading in all ungribbed files you need at the same time with fg_name.
ERROR: Missing values encountered in interpolated fields. Stopping.: probably not meteorological data covering the whole domain. Make domain smaller or get extra data.
If using ERA5 data, ensure SST and skintemp are interpolated correctly. Get the ERA5_INVARIANT file and updated METGRID.TBL from here.
Check interpolation around land mask using ncview! There should be no borders with values ~1e30.

General issues:

Check namelist.wps has the right names in the right places, the namelist.wps.all_options file shows where they should be (N.B. the optional geogrid path is wrong online).



Running WRF
real.exe issues:

not enough info for a p sfc computation: If it also says ERROR in psfc: flag_psfc = 1, flag_soilhgt = 0, flag_slp = 0, sfcp_to_sfcp = F, you need to find mean sea level pressure (slp) values and include them in metgrid.
not enough eta levels to reach p_top: just make e_vert higher or lower p_top_requested as suggested in the output.
Could not find level above ground: surface pressure is probably negative in some areas e.g. because the surface pressure used is from ERA5-Land so is not valid for sea. Fix this by using PSFC which is valid everywhere (e.g. from ERA5 hourly data on single levels).
grid%tsk unreasonable error and values of ~1e30: metgrid has interpolated the skin temperature values (which are over land) or the SST values (which are over water) badly or used the wrong mask for them. Ensure constants_name = 'ERA5_INVARIANT' is in &metgrid and use the METGRID_ERA5.TBL from here to correct masking. Even a non-fatal error in grid%tsk in rsl.out.0000 is still wrong! Suck it up, go back to metgrid, and fix it - even if wrfinput_d01 looks fine!
Program not doing anything: your code changes probably screwed everything, even if you only changed something you believed was part of wrf.exe.

wrf.exe issues:

For running with multiple CPUs, MPI must be executed explicitly with mpiexec -np num_cpus ./wrf.exe. mpirun is used interchangeably with mpiexec. To check it has run with multiple CPUs, look for rsl files in the em_real folder.
Segmentation fault: may be using too few cpus, the WRF forums say “((e_we)/100) * ((e_sn)/100) = least amount of processors you should use”
Program not doing anything: your code changes probably screwed everything.
Other segmentation errors or floating point exceptions:

Sometimes input data issues

General issues:

If running MPI, do a square number of CPUs since WRF prefers this.
You can normally get away with using fewer CPUs than suggested, but change it if it crashes.
Ensure time step follows \(dt\) (s) \(\leq 6 \cdot dx\) (km) and radiation time step follows \(dt\) (min) \(\leq dx\) (km), though you can normally get away with higher.
Don’t compile with full debugging option -D (i.e. with floating point exception errors etc) because the radar module will crash! Raised as an issue 2025-09-23 (see here). Even after this was fixed, the -D option is still prone to breaking. Try recompiling individual WRF files with debugging flags instead by identifying the compilation line in compile.log and adding debug flags to it.

title: Induction
text:
This page is intended to give an overview of the things everyone in AEIS, but in particular new members, should know.
AEIS is a research group within the Department of Aeronautics at Imperial. We have group meetings once a week to either share updates or present to each other.
Everyone in the group works on similar research, so this wiki contains our institutional knowledge which is useful to be shared between all of us. You may find information on the Data and Tools you use on those pages. You’ll also find tips on Writing and which Courses to take at Imperial.
AEIS has a Junior Leadership Team (JLT) with has a lead and a deputy for each of the following topics:

Group Meetings
Data & Computation
Sustainability

You can find more information on them here.

Offices, key cards, and desks
The AEIS group is currently split across a few offices, but we’ll hopefully be consolidated into 210 in the near future.
When you join, someone from the Aeronautics administration team (likely Lisa if you’re staff or Clodagh if you’re a PhD student, both in 318) will find you a desk and give access to your Imperial ID card. If you have issues, ask one of them or another member of the group. The department famously has a never-ending struggle to find desk space for everyone, so don’t be concerned if it takes a while.


Expenses
You can find most of the information you need to know about expenses on the department website. If you have questions about expenses, you can ask Ela at aero.finance@imperial.ac.uk.
You can make claims for small expenses by following the guidelines above.
For travel expenses, you should ask Ela (aero.finance@imperial.ac.uk) to register you with the College’s travel provider Egencia. To book travel with Egencia, request a Purchase Order (PO) number from Ela by sending a screenshot from Egencia with the travel details (including dates, price, etc), details on the purpose of the travel, and the account code which should be charged. If you don’t know your travel account code, again ask Ela. PhD students should CC Seb in the PO email.


Hardware, compute, and data surveys
The Data & Computation and Sustainability leads send out a hardware, compute, and data survey to the group every three months. This helps us keep a track of things like:

What computational resources we’re using
What data we’re storing
Whether we need support to make our computation easier
Whether there are any steps we can take to share information or consolidate resources

It helps make our work more focused and sustainable and is part of our Green DiSC requirements, so please do engage with it when reminded!


Data storage cleaning
Similar to above, the Data & Computation and Sustainability leads conduct data storage cleaning every three months. During this, each member of the group organises their storage directories (end-user, HPC, and cloud), identifies and deletes data they no longer need, and consolidates or minimises data they do need where possible.
This also helps make our work more focused and sustainable and is part of our Green DiSC requirements.


Computational sustainability
Please familiarise yourself with the best practices for computational sustainability. It’s best to put these practices in place as soon as possible because it’s not only more sustainable, but makes your work easier too. It will also make the hardware, compute, and data survey plus data storage cleaning simpler!


Wellbeing
If you need support or have concerns about anything or anyone including people within AEIS, there are lots of people at Imperial who can help you. Here are some details you might find useful.
General:

There are mental health first aiders across the department including

Lisa Kelly - l.kelly@imperial.ac.uk
Jackie O’Neill - j.oneill@imperial.ac.uk
Professor Joaquim Peiro - j.peiro@imperial.ac.uk

College-wide mental health first aiders
Department of Aeronautics staff wellbeing page

PhD students:

Student wellbeing adviser: Joe Kilbride, j.kilbride@imperial.ac.uk, Level 1, Room 141B, CAGB
Postgraduate research senior tutor: Professor Joaquim Peiro, j.peiro@imperial.ac.uk
Tutor for women: Dr Maria Ribera Vicent, m.ribera-vicent@imperial.ac.uk
Faculty of Engineering confidential support for BAME students: Naomi Jackson-Macfarlane, n.jackson-macfarlane@imperial.ac.uk
Student representatives
Department of Aeronautics postgraduate student wellbeing page

Finally, PhD Donuts takes place once a month for PhD students (very important for wellbeing) and there’s a coffee machine in both the Level 3 staff room and the kitchenette on Level 1.

title: Sustainability
text:
AEIS is committed to environmental sustainability. As a group, we aim to minimise the environmental impact of aviation using computational methods, so it is important to us to ensure the environmental benefits of producing our research (such as improvements in technology and changes in policy) outweigh the negative environmental impacts. For this reason, we have guidelines for AEIS group members to follow in two of the most relevant areas: Computation and Travel.
Contact the current AEIS group sustainability lead if you have any questions (see JLT). It is the sustainability lead’s role to develop, disseminate, and encourage sustainable practices in the group and to pursue sustainability accreditation.

title: Sustainability
text:
Best practices
If you have suggestions for tips to be added to this list, contact the sustainability lead!

Don’t replace devices unless necessary
Use your devices for longer. Even delaying a laptop upgrade for 1 or 2 years has an impact. Also, if your device breaks, try to get it repaired and source used or refurbished devices where possible.


Optimise your code
If you’ve written some code which is computationally demanding or that you’ll run for a long time, spend some time trying to make it more efficient. A more efficient program also means you get your results faster and can add up in the long term! GenAI models can be helpful for this.






CautionThe Jevons paradox: Greater efficiency -> greater consumption?





The Jevons paradox is the phenomenon whereby increasing the efficiency of a resource’s use increases the overall consumption of the resource. It has been seen observed for more than a century in various fields such as the increase in efficiency of coal use which made coal more attractive as a fuel and so increased its consumption. In your work, don’t let the improved efficiency of your code be an excuse for running it unnecessarily!





Debug on a small scale
When you’ve written a new model or some complex new code, you should debug it on a small scale before attempting to run it fully.
Compile with debug flags (for compiled code). Search for the options available for your compiler. For example, GCC users can use this page. CMake has cross-platform default flags which it uses when you use the argument -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug, but you can also customise them with set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG [YOUR FLAGS]). Other build platforms typically have debug options built in.
Test your code on a subset of input data when you first run it. This way, you won’t waste resources and energy finding the same bugs.
Profile your code to pinpoint bottlenecks with tools such as cProfile, py-spy, and perf. Add these tools into your workflow early so it feels natural and easy to do every time you need it.
Use a debugger if things are going wrong in your tests. Debuggers like GDB and Valgrind can be lifesavers in identifying segmentation faults, memory corruption, and fatal errors. You can set breakpoints and check the value of variables during runtime.
Once you’ve done this, you’ll be ready to scale up with confidence.


Request the resources you need
This applies to people using HPC platforms. It can be hard to know the resource needs of your code before you first run it, but once you have run it successfully, you can find out what resources it uses in the job logs (CPU percentage, memory usage, and runtime). Use this information to update your requests for the next time.


Only run simulations and data analysis once
It can be tempting to make small changes to models, pipelines, or data analysis which mean you need to run computationally expensive code again. Instead, consider carefully whether your code is finished before you run it and test your code on a small amount of data first to check it works. There are often things you’ll remember or discover which mean you don’t have to rerun expensive code.


Only store the data you need
It’s easy to let data pile up which you don’t need to keep. As a reference, storing 1 TB of data on the cloud consumes an estimated 40 to 70 kWh per year which is equivalent to running a modern refrigerator for an entire month (source, though I’ll look for better ones).
Where possible, don’t store preprocessed data when you have already processed the results and avoid storing multiple copies of the same data. If someone else uses the same data, share a single copy with them which you can both read from.
There are lots of tools which can help you identify data to delete such as WizTree on Windows and the du command on Linux. For a cross-platform tool designed for saving storage space, see fss.
AEIS runs quarterly data storage cleaning to encourage good practice.


Calculate your computational carbon footprint
The Green Algorithms calculator compares the carbon footprint of your code to tree-months of carbon sequestration, kilometres in a car, and fraction of a flight. It can help to have a reference point for the computational work you do so that we better understand the impact we’re having. Give it a try with the details of a job you’ve run.


GenAI
Generative AI (GenAI) is an invaluable tool to many of us. It is particularly useful for optimising your code. We will have more details on how to use GenAI effectively and how to account for its environmental impact soon.

title: Sustainability
text:
Green DiSC
Green DiSC (Digital Sustainability Certification) is an open-access scheme led by the University of Cambridge. It is designed to encourage people working in research to consider and minimise their computational environmental impact. It has three targets: research groups, research computing infrastructure teams, and central teams, of which the first is relevant to us. The certification has (or will have) three levels: Bronze, Silver, and Gold.
Its priorities for research groups are:

Purchasing and e-waste policies
Computing hardware and infrastructure inventory
Computational resource use
Dataset inventory and regular data storage cleaning
Knowledge amongst group members of best practices for computational sustainability (see Best practices!)

Timeline:

July 2026: Jack Bartlett enrolled AEIS with Green DiSC.
November 2026: Apply for Green DiSC Bronze certification.

Seb is the group’s Green DiSC representative, but the sustainability lead and deputy are in charge of pursuing the certification.
Useful links:

Green DiSC homepage
Green DiSC GitHub
Green Algorithms

title: About
text:
AEIS (the Aerospace Environmental Impacts Simulation group, pronounced “ace”) is a research group within the Department of Aeronautics, Faculty of Engineering, at Imperial. We use models and observations to understand and reduce the impacts of aviation on the environment.
You can find more information about AEIS, our members, and what we get up to on our Imperial webpage.
Information on group meetings can be found here.
